Vinyl-addition polymerizations of cycloallenes:
synthetic access to congeners of cyclic-ole ﬁn
polymers†
Nicholas J. Galan, ‡ Justin M. Burroughs, ‡ Christopher R. Maroon, Brian K. Long
and Johnathan N. Brantley
 *
Expanding the scope of cycloole ﬁn-type monomers that polymer-
ize via coordination–insertion mechanisms is an enduring syn-
thetic challenge. Vinyl-addition polymerizations of cyclic ole ﬁns
are almost exclusively limited to norbornene sca ﬀolds and/or
copolymerizations with ethylene. To circumvent these synthetic
limitations, we report the vinyl-addition polymerization of cycloal-
lenes using the catalyst, [( π-allyl)NiOCOCF
3]2. The polycyclic
materials could be accessed in excellent yields (up to 97%), and
the polymerization exhibited living character (which was leveraged
for copolymerizations with acyclic monomers). Importantly, we
found that multiple ring sizes could be incorporated into polymer
architectures, and material properties could be tailored by control-
ling the cycloallene feed ratios.
Relative to their acyclic congeners, cycloolefin polymers are
enticing synthetic targets that frequently exhibit unique physi-
cal properties. Indeed, the incorporation of small carbocyclic
motifs into soft materials can impact optical transparency,
1,2
modify viscosity, 3 increase Tg,4 and enhance the modulus. 5 In
principle, cyclic motifs can be introduced into polymer
matrices through a variety of polymerization manifolds;
however, practical considerations often narrow the scope of
applicable methods. For example, radical and ionic polymeriz-
ations can undergo deleterious chain termination events or
undesired rearrangements (resulting in low yields and oligo-
meric products).
6,7 Furthermore, ring-opening polymerizations
typically require highly strained monomers ( e.g. norbornene),
which intrinsically limits monomer scope.
Vinyl-addition polymerizations of cyclic olefins typically
exhibit improved performance, but such polymerizations are
not without synthetic obstacles. For example, vinyl-addition
homopolymerizations of cyclic olefins other than norbornene
and cyclopentene are virtually unknown.
8 Although many
cyclic olefins can be copolymerized with ethylene, this strategy
usually requires highly reactive catalysts (which can exhibit
poor functional group tolerance) and harsh co-catalysts or acti-
vators (Scheme 1). Given these limitations, exploring new
monomer and catalyst space is imperative for overcoming
these obstacles.
Much like their olefin congeners, allenes polymerize under
a variety of conditions
9 (e.g. radical,10 cationic,11 anionic,12
and coordination–insertion13–16). We were particularly inspired
by the work of Endo and colleagues, who have shown that

[(π-allyl)NiOCOCF3]2 (3; Scheme 1) catalyzes the living polymer-
ization of allenes bearing an array of functional groups ( e.g.
alcohols,17 esters,18 or amides, 19). One brief report by Endo
and colleagues revealed that catalyst 3 can facilitate the
polymerization of cycloallenes; however, this succinct note
lacked detailed analyses of polymerization kinetics, living
character at higher conversions, copolymerizations, or bulk
material properties.
20 As these materials can be considered
analogues of cycloolefin polymers, we envisioned that a more
detailed study of their syntheses and properties could reveal
important design elements for creating a spate of advanced
architectures. Indeed, cycloolefins can be e ﬃciently trans-
formed into cycloallenes using the two-step Skattebøl
rearrangement.
21 This operationally simple strategy, combined
with a deeper understanding of cycloallene polymerization
tendencies and the functional group tolerance of 3, could sig-
nificantly expand the scope of potential monomers
22 for vinyl-
addition polymerizations. Given these considerations, we envi-
sioned that vinyl-addition polymerizations of cyclic allenes
would a ﬀord access to novel derivatives of cycloolefin (co)
polymers.
We selected 1,2-cyclononadiene ( 1) as our model substrate,
given that (i) it is easily synthesized from cyclooctene on a
multi-gram scale, and (ii) the resultant polymer would contain
rings that are di ﬃcult to incorporate using traditional mono-
mers.
23 Our initial studies commenced with the homopoly-
merization of 1 using catalyst 3 (Scheme 1). Gratifyingly, the
polymerization proceeded rapidly ( vide infra )t oa ﬀord the
desired polymer, 2, as a white powder in excellent yield (94%,
Table 1). Analysis by gel-permeation chromatography (GPC)
revealed that polymer 2 exhibited low dispersity ( Đ = 1.11) and
a number-average molecular weight ( M
n = 36 kDa) similar to
the targeted value. We note that we consistently observed a
high molecular weight impurity that we were unable to
avoid.
24 Thermogravimetric analysis of 2 revealed a relatively
high decomposition temperature ( Td = 350 °C), which is com-
parable to cycloolefin polymers. 25 Unfortunately, we were
unable to observe any thermal transitions using di ﬀerential
scanning calorimetry.
The predicted 26 ring strain of 1 is typical for other 9-mem-
bered rings ( ∼12 kcal mol −1); thus, the rapid polymerization
we observed suggested that unusually high strain may not be
required to access our target materials. To benchmark this, we
monitored homopolymerizations of 1 and an acyclic analogue,
1,2-nonadiene ( 7), via 1H NMR spectroscopy (see ESI †). We
observed >95% conversion of 1 within 20 min, compared to
approximately 60 min for >95% consumption of 7.
Furthermore, 1 exhibited a 6-fold increase in polymerization
rate relative to 7 (cf. kobs = 0.296 for 1 versus kobs = 0.052 for 7;
Fig. 1). These studies demonstrate that modestly-strained
cycloallenes possess enhanced reactivity relative to acyclic
allenes. This behaviour starkly contrasts cyclic olefin polymer-
ization tendencies, and these promising results suggest that
our strategy could accommodate monomers bearing larger
ring sizes ( vide infra).
Having identified 3 as a highly active catalyst, we sought to
further optimize the polymerization. We began our studies by
examining other vinyl-addition polymerization catalysts
27 (4–6;
Scheme 1). Although 1 polymerized in the presence of catalyst
4, GPC analysis revealed that the Mn of the isolated material
was significantly higher than the theoretical value (Table 1).
Polymerizations in the presence of catalyst 5 (activated with
AgSbF6) required lengthy reaction times (24 h), whereas cata-
lyst 6 (also activated with AgSbF 6)a ﬀorded low yields of highly
insoluble materials (Table 1). The addition of AgSbF 6 to 3
(which is known to enhance the activity of Ni based catalysts 27)
resulted in materials with low Mn and broad Đ. Finally, poly-
merizations at elevated temperatures (35, 50, and 65 °C)

which we hypothesize may be due to catalyst decomposition
(Table 1).
With our selected polymerization conditions in hand, we
next evaluated the living character of these polymerizations.
Briefly, aliquots were periodically removed during the polymer-
ization of 1 and quenched by exposure to air. Monomer con-
version was determined via
1H NMR spectroscopy, and Mn and
Đ values were determined by GPC. As shown in Fig. 2, a linear
correlation between Mn and monomer conversion was
observed while maintaining relatively narrow dispersities ( Đ ≤
1.2). Moreover, chain extension via sequential addition of 1
was successful (see ESI for more details †), further supporting
the living nature of this polymerization (Fig. 2). Importantly,
these data suggest that cycloallenes may be readily integrated
into an array of soft materials through copolymerizations.
Given that polymers containing cyclic motifs often exhibit
unique thermomechanical properties, we sought to investigate
the e ﬀect of cycloallene-derived moieties on mechanical pro-
perties ( i.e. Young’s modulus). In a preliminary study, we syn-
thesized a series of high M
n (∼100 kDa) statistical copolymers
by varying the feed ratio of 1 : 7 (70 : 30, 50 : 50, and 30 : 70;
Table 2). These materials were then cast into films from CHCl 3
and used for subsequent tensile testing. We surmised that
increased cycloallene content would result in an increased
Young’s modulus (in direct analogy to reports of more tra-
ditional cycloolefin copolymers). 28 Conversely, we expected
increased acyclic allene content would lower the modulus [in
direct analogy to poly( α-olefins)].
Tension tests were conducted for materials containing 70
and 50 mol% 1. The homopolymer of 1 proved too brittle for
analysis, whereas both the homopolymer of 7 and the
30 mol% copolymer proved too tacky for mechanical analysis.
We measured a Young ’s modulus of 1367 ± 15 MPa [strain at
break = 2.5% (±0.6%)] for the 70 mol% polymer (Fig. 3).
Conversely, tensile testing of the 50 mol% material revealed a
Young’s modulus of 263 ± 30 MPa [strain at break = 5.2%
(±2.4%)]. These data are consistent with observations from
cyclic olefin polymers,
28 and they demonstrate that relatively
modest changes in cycloallene feed ratios can dramatically
impact the mechanical properties of the resultant materials.
Slouf reported similar trends in copolymers with varied nor-
bornene content (15 –30% norbornene),
29 which further illus-
trates the apparent similarity between cycloolefin and cycloal-
lene polymers. Although preliminary, these results suggest
that our approach could be amenable to synthesizing a spate
of soft materials with highly tunable physical properties.
Finally, we sought to demonstrate the compatibility of our
polymerization strategy with other cycloallene ring sizes.
Synthesizing materials with large ring sizes is inherently
diﬃcult,
30 with cycloolefin sca ﬀolds being limited primarily to
fused polycycles ( e.g. tetracyclododecene). However, increased
ring sizes could further modify bulk material properties, such
as Td
31 or modulus. 28 We prepared 1,2-cyclotridecadiene ( 8)
and subjected it to our optimized polymerization conditions
(ESI†). Interestingly, the polymerization of 8 required longer
reaction times (72 h) to achieve modest conversions (67%),
which is likely due to the steric hindrance of incorporating
13-membered rings into the growing polymer chain. The resul-
tant material exhibited poor solubility in common solvents
(CHCl
3, DCM, THF, PhMe, etc.); however, some portions could
be dissolved in CDCl 3, and subsequent 1H NMR spectroscopic
analysis was consistent with the proposed polymer (ESI †).
Molecular weight data could only be determined using high-
temperature GPC, which revealed that we could access rela-
tively high M
n polymers despite the sluggish nature of the
polymerization ( Mn = 47 289; Đ = 1.99). Although further work
is needed, these preliminary studies demonstrate that lower
strain cyclic motifs can successfully be incorporated into
polymer matrices.
In conclusion, we have demonstrated that vinyl-addition
polymerization of cycloallenes is a potentially valuable strategy

Importantly, cycloallenes can be polymerized in a well-con-

This route does not require high strain monomers ( e.g. norbor-
nene) to achieve cyclic motif incorporation, and copolymeriza-
tion with acyclic monomers is possible (but not required to
achieve good conversion). Taken together, these results
suggest that vinyl-addition polymerizations of cyclic allenes
could provide a reliable synthetic route toward heretofore inac-
cessible materials.

[(π-allyl)NiOCOCF3]2 (3; Scheme 1) catalyzes the living polymer-
ization of allenes bearing an array of functional groups ( e.g.
alcohols,17 esters,18 or amides, 19). One brief report by Endo
and colleagues revealed that catalyst 3 can facilitate the
polymerization of cycloallenes; however, this succinct note
lacked detailed analyses of polymerization kinetics, living
character at higher conversions, copolymerizations, or bulk
material properties.
20 As these materials can be considered
analogues of cycloolefin polymers, we envisioned that a more
detailed study of their syntheses and properties could reveal
important design elements for creating a spate of advanced
architectures. Indeed, cycloolefins can be e ﬃciently trans-
formed into cycloallenes using the two-step Skattebøl
rearrangement.
21 This operationally simple strategy, combined
with a deeper understanding of cycloallene polymerization
tendencies and the functional group tolerance of 3, could sig-
nificantly expand the scope of potential monomers
22 for vinyl-
addition polymerizations. Given these considerations, we envi-
sioned that vinyl-addition polymerizations of cyclic allenes
would a ﬀord access to novel derivatives of cycloolefin (co)
polymers.
We selected 1,2-cyclononadiene ( 1) as our model substrate,
given that (i) it is easily synthesized from cyclooctene on a
multi-gram scale, and (ii) the resultant polymer would contain
rings that are di ﬃcult to incorporate using traditional mono-
mers.
23 Our initial studies commenced with the homopoly-
merization of 1 using catalyst 3 (Scheme 1). Gratifyingly, the
polymerization proceeded rapidly ( vide infra )t oa ﬀord the
desired polymer, 2, as a white powder in excellent yield (94%,
Table 1). Analysis by gel-permeation chromatography (GPC)
revealed that polymer 2 exhibited low dispersity ( Đ = 1.11) and
a number-average molecular weight ( M
n = 36 kDa) similar to
the targeted value. We note that we consistently observed a
high molecular weight impurity that we were unable to
avoid.
24 Thermogravimetric analysis of 2 revealed a relatively
high decomposition temperature ( Td = 350 °C), which is com-
parable to cycloolefin polymers. 25 Unfortunately, we were
unable to observe any thermal transitions using di ﬀerential
scanning calorimetry.
The predicted 26 ring strain of 1 is typical for other 9-mem-
bered rings ( ∼12 kcal mol −1); thus, the rapid polymerization
we observed suggested that unusually high strain may not be
required to access our target materials. To benchmark this, we
monitored homopolymerizations of 1 and an acyclic analogue,
1,2-nonadiene ( 7), via 1H NMR spectroscopy (see ESI †). We
observed >95% conversion of 1 within 20 min, compared to
approximately 60 min for >95% consumption of 7.
Furthermore, 1 exhibited a 6-fold increase in polymerization
rate relative to 7 (cf. kobs = 0.296 for 1 versus kobs = 0.052 for 7;
Fig. 1). These studies demonstrate that modestly-strained
cycloallenes possess enhanced reactivity relative to acyclic
allenes. This behaviour starkly contrasts cyclic olefin polymer-
ization tendencies, and these promising results suggest that
our strategy could accommodate monomers bearing larger
ring sizes ( vide infra).
Having identified 3 as a highly active catalyst, we sought to
further optimize the polymerization. We began our studies by
examining other vinyl-addition polymerization catalysts
27 (4–6;
Scheme 1). Although 1 polymerized in the presence of catalyst
4, GPC analysis revealed that the Mn of the isolated material
was significantly higher than the theoretical value (Table 1).
Polymerizations in the presence of catalyst 5 (activated with
AgSbF6) required lengthy reaction times (24 h), whereas cata-
lyst 6 (also activated with AgSbF 6)a ﬀorded low yields of highly
insoluble materials (Table 1). The addition of AgSbF 6 to 3
(which is known to enhance the activity of Ni based catalysts 27)
resulted in materials with low Mn and broad Đ. Finally, poly-
merizations at elevated temperatures (35, 50, and 65 °C)
aﬀorded materials with (i) Mn values that exceeded the theore-

With our selected polymerization conditions in hand, we
next evaluated the living character of these polymerizations.
Briefly, aliquots were periodically removed during the polymer-
ization of 1 and quenched by exposure to air. Monomer con-
version was determined via
1H NMR spectroscopy, and Mn and
Đ values were determined by GPC. As shown in Fig. 2, a linear
correlation between Mn and monomer conversion was
observed while maintaining relatively narrow dispersities ( Đ ≤
1.2). Moreover, chain extension via sequential addition of 1
was successful (see ESI for more details †), further supporting
the living nature of this polymerization (Fig. 2). Importantly,
these data suggest that cycloallenes may be readily integrated
into an array of soft materials through copolymerizations.
Given that polymers containing cyclic motifs often exhibit
unique thermomechanical properties, we sought to investigate
the e ﬀect of cycloallene-derived moieties on mechanical pro-
perties ( i.e. Young’s modulus). In a preliminary study, we syn-
thesized a series of high M
n (∼100 kDa) statistical copolymers
by varying the feed ratio of 1 : 7 (70 : 30, 50 : 50, and 30 : 70;
Table 2). These materials were then cast into films from CHCl 3
and used for subsequent tensile testing. We surmised that
increased cycloallene content would result in an increased
Young’s modulus (in direct analogy to reports of more tra-
ditional cycloolefin copolymers). 28 Conversely, we expected
increased acyclic allene content would lower the modulus [in
direct analogy to poly( α-olefins)].
Tension tests were conducted for materials containing 70
and 50 mol% 1. The homopolymer of 1 proved too brittle for
analysis, whereas both the homopolymer of 7 and the
30 mol% copolymer proved too tacky for mechanical analysis.
We measured a Young ’s modulus of 1367 ± 15 MPa [strain at
break = 2.5% (±0.6%)] for the 70 mol% polymer (Fig. 3).
Conversely, tensile testing of the 50 mol% material revealed a
Young’s modulus of 263 ± 30 MPa [strain at break = 5.2%
(±2.4%)]. These data are consistent with observations from
cyclic olefin polymers,
28 and they demonstrate that relatively
modest changes in cycloallene feed ratios can dramatically
impact the mechanical properties of the resultant materials.
Slouf reported similar trends in copolymers with varied nor-
bornene content (15 –30% norbornene),
29 which further illus-
trates the apparent similarity between cycloolefin and cycloal-
lene polymers. Although preliminary, these results suggest
that our approach could be amenable to synthesizing a spate
of soft materials with highly tunable physical properties.
Finally, we sought to demonstrate the compatibility of our
polymerization strategy with other cycloallene ring sizes.
Synthesizing materials with large ring sizes is inherently
diﬃcult,
30 with cycloolefin sca ﬀolds being limited primarily to
fused polycycles ( e.g. tetracyclododecene). However, increased
ring sizes could further modify bulk material properties, such
as Td
31 or modulus. 28 We prepared 1,2-cyclotridecadiene ( 8)
and subjected it to our optimized polymerization conditions
(ESI†). Interestingly, the polymerization of 8 required longer
reaction times (72 h) to achieve modest conversions (67%),
which is likely due to the steric hindrance of incorporating
13-membered rings into the growing polymer chain. The resul-
tant material exhibited poor solubility in common solvents
(CHCl
3, DCM, THF, PhMe, etc.); however, some portions could
be dissolved in CDCl 3, and subsequent 1H NMR spectroscopic
analysis was consistent with the proposed polymer (ESI †).
Molecular weight data could only be determined using high-
temperature GPC, which revealed that we could access rela-
tively high M
n polymers despite the sluggish nature of the
polymerization ( Mn = 47 289; Đ = 1.99). Although further work
is needed, these preliminary studies demonstrate that lower
strain cyclic motifs can successfully be incorporated into
polymer matrices.

polymerization of cycloallenes is a potentially valuable strategy

source_context.title: Vinyl-addition polymerizations of cycloallenes: synthetic access to congeners of cyclic-olefin polymers

observations: Table 1 entry 1 material: Mn 35.6 kDa and Đ 1.11 by GPC; a recurring high-Mn impurity was observed.
No thermal transitions were observed by differential scanning calorimetry.
Predicted ring strain of monomer 1 is approximately 12 kcal mol-1.
Materials were cast into films from CHCl3 for tensile testing.
70:30 feed material: Young's modulus 1367 ± 15 MPa; strain at break 2.5% ± 0.6%.
50:50 feed material: Young's modulus 263 ± 30 MPa; strain at break 5.2% ± 2.4%.
Homopolymer 1 was too brittle; homopolymer 7 and the 30 mol% 1 copolymer were too tacky for mechanical analysis.
Footnote 24 says a series of experiments tested oxidative chain-coupling or catalyst chain transfer as origins of the high-Mn species.
The studies did not identify the origin; experiment count and conditions are only in unprovided ESI and are not fabricated here.
